newsitem.title: PERU: Officer accused of MRTA security lapse leaves Peru.
newsitem.headline: Officer accused of MRTA security lapse leaves Peru.

text.p: The police chief charged as most responsible for the security lapse that allowed rebels to storm the Japanese ambassador's home violated a court order and left Peru, police sources said on Tuesday.

Lt. Gen. Luis Malasquez was the highest ranking of 19 policemen charged with negligence and disobedience over the attack. He flew out of Peru with his wife early on Sunday and was believed to be in Costa Rica or Mexico, the sources said.

Malasquez was in charge of police security in Lima in December when 14 jungle-trained Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels burst into a diplomatic reception, taking hundreds hostage. He was due to appear before the Supreme Military Court on Wednesday.
But the police general apparently received advanced warning of the court's order -- issued on Monday -- to prevent officers charged over the assault from leaving the country, the sources said.
If Malasquez does not attend Wednesday's hearing, Peru will be unable to extradite him because the country has no such laws governing his alleged military crimes, court officials said.

Last week, Interior Minister Gen. Cesar Saucedo said the National Intelligence Service and the armed forces were free from blame for the MRTA raid that saw much of Peru's security forces' top brass taken captive. But he pledged to punish the police officers held responsible.

Saucedo told Congress that despite ample evidence rebels planned to attack a diplomatic building, police had failed to give priority to the Dec. 17 cocktail party or coordinate with Japanese staff to provide adequate security.

But police reports obtained by Reuters show the force believes it is being made the scapegoat for the MRTA attack, claiming it warned the armed forces of the risks in allowing many of its senior officials to attend the reception.
The minister's accusations against the police were to "protect certain vested interests," Malasquez said without elaborating, according to local press reports last week.

Police chief Ketin Vidal and the then Interior Minister Gen. Juan Briones Davila resigned just three days before the armed forces mounted its April 22 assault that freed all but one of the MRTA's 72 hostages.
Two commandos and all of the rebels died in an explosive raid launched from tunnels under the mansion while the MRTA rebels played indoor soccer.
